summary.name: Building On-Call Culture at GitHub
summary.one_liner: A GitHub engineering blog post describing how the company split its monolithic, hero-based on-call rotation so each engineering team carries on-call duty for the code it owns.
use_cases: Redesigning an on-call rotation for a large monolithic codebase
Mapping code files and alerts to owning teams
Planning on-call training and onboarding for engineers
Reducing on-call burden and alert noise
Building a blameless incident response culture
summary.what_it_does: The post explains why GitHub moved from one large 24-hour on-call rotation for its Ruby on Rails monolith to per-team on-call. It describes the pain points of the old model, such as engineers being paged rarely and lacking context, noisy alerts and poor runbooks, and a small group of experts handling every incident. It then covers the logistics: mapping over 16,000 files to services and services to teams, a Service Catalog for lookup, a linter that requires ownership information, and splitting monolith-wide alerts among teams. It also covers the cultural work: training rounds, office hours, work-life balance during on-call, and blamelessness. The post reports that incident resolution time improved after most of the change, but describes the effort as ongoing.
notable: Per-file to service to team ownership mapping, enforced by a linter that blocks changes lacking ownership info
In-house Service Catalog that lets engineers, support and product find which team owns a service
Allows teams roughly 20% of time for technical debt and 20% for on-call experience improvements
Each of over 50 teams tracked through a GitHub issue with checklists
caveats: This is a company case study, not a downloadable tool; the Service Catalog is internal to GitHub
Describes cultural change that the author says will take years and is not fully resolved
